hints: Look carefully at the scale bar and notice where 100 nm, 1 µm and 100 µm sit, prokaryotes are tiny but not as tiny as molecules.
Remember the typical diameter of a bacterium like E. coli is about 1 µm, so ask which bracket is centred on 1 µm.
walkthrough:
**Read the size scale**

Think of this as a zoom from very, very small on the left to visible on the right.

Remember the conversions:
$$1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ µm} = 1,000,000 \text{ nm}$$

**Recall typical cell sizes**

Prokaryotic cells like bacteria are much smaller than most eukaryotic cells.
A good rule to remember is most bacteria are about $0.5$ to $5 \text{ µm}$ in diameter, often quoted as around $1 \text{ µm}$.

**Match to the brackets**

Bracket A (1 nm to 100 nm) is virus and large molecule size, far too small for a whole cell.
Bracket B is centred on $1 \text{ µm}$, so it catches most prokaryotes. Brackets C and D are $1 \text{ µm}$ to $1 \text{ mm}$, which is mainly eukaryotic cell and visible size.

options.A: Too small, 1 nm to 100 nm is the size of molecules, membranes and viruses, not whole prokaryotic cells.
options.B: Correct, this range spans about 100 nm to a few µm and is centred on 1 µm, which is the typical size of most bacteria.
options.C: Too large for most prokaryotes, this is the typical range for eukaryotic cells like plant and animal cells (about 10 to 100 µm).
options.D: Far too large, 100 µm to 1 mm approaches what you can see with the naked eye, much bigger than any typical bacterium.
